# Overview {#sec-overview}

## Purpose

This document is the consolidated data-processing pipeline for the
*Drinking Water and Environmental Justice* data brief (`drinking_water.qmd`).
It runs, end to end, every data-acquisition and processing step documented
in that brief's Methodology section:

1. **Service area boundaries** — EPA community water system service area
   polygons for Cook County (@sec-boundaries).
2. **Violation and compliance data** — EPA SDWIS/ECHO Safe Drinking Water
   Act records, summarized by water system and joined to the boundaries
   (@sec-sdwis).
3. **Lead service line inventories** — Illinois EPA's annual Service Line
   Material Inventory reports, standardized and joined to the service
   areas (@sec-lsl).

The final step (@sec-save) writes a single, lightweight `.RData` file
containing only the objects the *rendered data brief* actually needs.

## Rationale

`drinking_water.qmd` sets `eval: false` globally and shows its Methodology
chunks for documentation purposes only. Those chunks are not meant to be
re-run — and re-download more than 400 MB of EPA data — every time the
brief is rendered. Instead, this pipeline is run separately on a refresh
cadence, and the brief's single evaluated setup chunk (*load prepared
analysis data*) simply `load()`s this pipeline's output to make
`cook_county` and `cook_cws_with_violations` available to the Analysis
section's interactive leaflet map.

## Usage

Render (or run) this document with the working directory set to its own
folder (`scripts/qmd/`), which matches the relative `data/` paths used
throughout `drinking_water.qmd`. Quarto does this automatically when
rendering:

```bash
quarto render drinking_water_dataprep.qmd
```

To run the code without producing an HTML report, extract it to a plain R
script and source it from an R session started in `scripts/qmd/`:

```r
knitr::purl("drinking_water_dataprep.qmd")
source("drinking_water_dataprep.R")
```

## Outputs

All outputs are written under `scripts/qmd/data/`, and the folders are
created if missing. The pipeline also needs one input that must be
downloaded by hand: IEPA's `ServiceLineMaterialInventoryReports.csv`,
saved to the `data/` folder (see @sec-lsl).

| File | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `data/spatial/cook_county_water_system_boundaries.{gpkg,shp}` | Cook County community water system service areas |
| `data/spatial/cook_county_water_systems_with_violations.shp` | Service areas joined to system-level violation summaries |
| `data/tabular/cook_county_pws_inventory.csv` | Cook County public water system inventory |
| `data/tabular/cook_county_sdwa_violations.csv` | Decoded SDWA violations for Cook County systems |
| `data/tabular/cook_county_lead_copper_samples.csv` | Lead and Copper Rule sample results |
| `data/tabular/cook_county_pws_violation_summary.csv` | Violation counts summarized by water system |
| `data/tabular/cook_county_lsl_inventory_history.csv` | IEPA service line material inventories for Cook County systems, all reporting years |
| `data/tabular/cook_county_lsl_inventory_latest.csv` | Each system's most recent IEPA service line inventory |
| `data/tabular/cook_county_lsl_summary_by_year.csv` | Service line material totals across Cook County systems by reporting year |
| `data/drinking_water_dataprep.RData` | Essential objects loaded directly by `drinking_water.qmd` |

# Setup {#sec-setup}

## Load packages

The following chunk attaches the packages used throughout the pipeline,
with a short note on what each one is used for.

```{r}
#| label: load-packages

library(dplyr)      # data wrangling
library(tidyr)      # replace_na
library(stringr)    # str_starts, str_to_upper
library(readr)      # read_csv, write_csv
library(sf)         # spatial operations
library(httr2)      # ArcGIS REST Feature Service queries (see fetch_arcgis_features())
library(geojsonsf)  # parse ArcGIS REST GeoJSON responses into sf
library(tigris)     # counties()
library(ggplot2)    # quick visual QA plot
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why not `arcgislayers`?

This pipeline deliberately does **not** use the `arcgislayers` package.
`arcgislayers` requires `rlang >= 1.3.0`, and on systems where
administrative policy pins `rlang` to an older version (e.g. 1.1.7),
calling any `arcgislayers` function (even `arc_open()`) fails with
*"namespace 'rlang' ... is already loaded, but >= 1.3.0 is required"*.
`rlang` cannot be reloaded at a different version mid-session once another
attached package (`dplyr`, `tidyr`, etc.) has already loaded it. All ArcGIS
REST Feature Service access below instead goes through
`fetch_arcgis_features()` (`httr2` + `geojsonsf`; see @sec-arcgis-helpers),
which has no `rlang` version requirement beyond what `dplyr`/`tidyr`
already need.
:::

## Configure spatial engine and output paths

EPA's Public Water System Service Area Boundaries dataset includes some
invalid polygons (self-intersections, duplicate vertices), especially among
EPA-modeled boundaries. `sf`'s default spherical geometry engine (`s2`) is
strict about validity and will error on these, so the next chunk falls back
to the more forgiving GEOS planar engine for the duration of the pipeline.
Geometries are still explicitly repaired with `st_make_valid()` as a second
safeguard. The chunk also defines the output locations and creates the
output folders if they do not already exist.

```{r}
#| label: configure-environment

sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)

out_spatial_dir <- "data/spatial"
out_tabular_dir <- "data/tabular"
out_rdata_path  <- "data/drinking_water_dataprep.RData"

dir.create(out_spatial_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(out_tabular_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
```

# Public Water System Service Area Boundaries {#sec-boundaries}

This section mirrors the brief's Methodology subsection *Public Water
System Service Area Boundaries*. It retrieves community water system
service area polygons from EPA's hosted ArcGIS Feature Service and clips
them to Cook County.

**Source:** EPA Office of Water, [Public Water System Service Area
Boundaries v3](https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/public-water-system-service-areas).

The chunk below stores the Feature Service URL used throughout this
section.

```{r}
#| label: boundaries-feature-server-url

feature_server_url <- "https://services.arcgis.com/cJ9YHowT8TU7DUyn/arcgis/rest/services/Water_System_Boundaries/FeatureServer"
```

## Cook County boundary

The national boundaries dataset contains more than 44,000 systems. To avoid
downloading all of them, the Cook County polygon is retrieved from the
Census Bureau's cartographic boundary files (via `tigris`) and used as a
spatial filter. It is projected to WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) to match the Feature
Service.

```{r}
#| label: cook-county-boundary

cook_county <- counties(state = "IL", cb = TRUE, year = 2023) %>%
  filter(NAME == "Cook") %>%
  st_transform(4326)
```

## ArcGIS REST Feature Service helpers {#sec-arcgis-helpers}

These two helper functions cover everything `arcgislayers` would otherwise
provide for this pipeline: inspecting a FeatureServer's layer list, and
paginated feature retrieval with an optional bounding-box spatial filter.

### Listing available layers

`print_arcgis_layers()` is a lightweight replacement for `arc_open()` +
`print()`. It fetches and prints the FeatureServer's layer listing so the
correct layer index can be confirmed (a service may expose more than one
layer, e.g. active vs. historical).

```{r}
#| label: fn-print-arcgis-layers

print_arcgis_layers <- function(base_url) {
  service_info <- request(base_url) %>%
    req_url_query(f = "json") %>%
    req_perform() %>%
    resp_body_json()

  layers <- service_info$layers
  if (length(layers) == 0) {
    message("No layers reported for ", base_url)
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }

  message("Layers available on ", base_url, ":")
  for (lyr in layers) {
    message(sprintf("  [%s] %s", lyr$id, lyr$name))
  }
  invisible(service_info)
}
```

### Paginated feature retrieval

`fetch_arcgis_features()` replaces `arc_select()`. It queries an ArcGIS
REST Feature Service layer and returns the result as an `sf` object. Esri
REST services usually cap each response at roughly 1,000–2,000 records
(`maxRecordCount`), so the function pages through results with
`resultOffset` until a short or empty page signals the last one. When
`geometry_sf` is supplied, its bounding box is sent as a cheap server-side
prefilter (mirroring `arc_select(filter_geom = ...)`); callers refine the
result afterward with an exact `st_filter()`.

```{r}
#| label: fn-fetch-arcgis-features

fetch_arcgis_features <- function(base_url, layer_id = 0, where = "1=1",
                                   out_fields = "*", geometry_sf = NULL,
                                   batch_size = 1000) {
  query_url <- paste0(base_url, "/", layer_id, "/query")

  # Bounding-box prefilter (server-side), refined with st_filter() afterward.
  geom_param <- NULL
  if (!is.null(geometry_sf)) {
    bb <- st_bbox(st_transform(geometry_sf, 4326))
    geom_param <- sprintf(
      '{"xmin":%f,"ymin":%f,"xmax":%f,"ymax":%f,"spatialReference":{"wkid":4326}}',
      bb["xmin"], bb["ymin"], bb["xmax"], bb["ymax"]
    )
  }

  all_features <- list()
  offset <- 0
  repeat {
    req <- request(query_url) %>%
      req_url_query(
        where = where,
        outFields = out_fields,
        f = "geojson",
        resultOffset = offset,
        resultRecordCount = batch_size,
        geometry = geom_param,
        geometryType = if (!is.null(geom_param)) "esriGeometryEnvelope" else NULL,
        inSR = if (!is.null(geom_param)) 4326 else NULL,
        spatialRel = if (!is.null(geom_param)) "esriSpatialRelIntersects" else NULL
      )

    resp <- req_perform(req)
    txt <- resp_body_string(resp)

    batch_sf <- geojson_sf(txt)
    if (nrow(batch_sf) == 0) break

    all_features[[length(all_features) + 1]] <- batch_sf
    if (nrow(batch_sf) < batch_size) break
    offset <- offset + batch_size
  }

  if (length(all_features) == 0) {
    return(all_features)  # empty list -- caller decides how to handle
  }

  dplyr::bind_rows(all_features) %>%
    st_as_sf() %>%
    st_make_valid()
}
```

## Retrieve Cook County community water system boundaries

First, the FeatureServer's layers are listed to confirm that layer `0` is
the main community water system boundaries layer.

```{r}
#| label: list-boundary-layers

print_arcgis_layers(feature_server_url)
```

Next, only features whose bounding box intersects the Cook County boundary
are pulled from layer `0`. The pipeline stops with an informative error if
nothing is returned, since every later step depends on these boundaries.

```{r}
#| label: fetch-boundaries

cook_cws_raw <- fetch_arcgis_features(
  base_url    = feature_server_url,
  layer_id    = 0,
  geometry_sf = cook_county
)

if (length(cook_cws_raw) == 0 || nrow(cook_cws_raw) == 0) {
  stop("No community water system boundary features were returned for the ",
       "Cook County bounding box -- check feature_server_url and the ",
       "FeatureServer's availability before continuing.")
}
```

Finally, invalid geometries are repaired, any features that remain invalid
are dropped (with a message reporting how many), and the result is clipped
precisely to the Cook County polygon.

```{r}
#| label: clean-clip-boundaries

cook_cws_valid <- cook_cws_raw %>%
  st_make_valid()

n_invalid <- sum(!st_is_valid(cook_cws_valid))
if (n_invalid > 0) {
  message(n_invalid, " feature(s) remain invalid after st_make_valid(); ",
          "these will be dropped before clipping.")
  cook_cws_valid <- cook_cws_valid[st_is_valid(cook_cws_valid), ]
}

cook_cws <- cook_cws_valid %>%
  st_filter(cook_county, .predicate = st_intersects)  # precise clip to county polygon
```

## Save and quality check

The next chunk prints a compact summary of the boundary attributes and
writes the boundaries to both GeoPackage and Shapefile formats.

```{r}
#| label: save-boundaries

glimpse(st_drop_geometry(cook_cws))

st_write(cook_cws, file.path(out_spatial_dir, "cook_county_water_system_boundaries.gpkg"),
          delete_dsn = TRUE)
st_write(cook_cws, file.path(out_spatial_dir, "cook_county_water_system_boundaries.shp"),
          delete_dsn = TRUE)
```

As a quick visual check, the service areas are mapped within the Cook
County outline, with each system shaded a different color.

```{r}
#| label: fig-boundaries-qa
#| fig-cap: "Community water system service areas, Cook County, IL"

print(
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = cook_county, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_sf(data = cook_cws, aes(fill = PWS_Name), color = "white", linewidth = 0.1,
            show.legend = FALSE, alpha = 0.85) +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(
      title = "Community Water System Service Areas, Cook County, IL",
      caption = "Source: U.S. EPA Public Water System Service Area Boundaries (v3)"
    )
)
```

## Notes

- This layer covers **community** water systems only. Non-community systems
  (schools, gas stations, small transient supplies) are published in a
  separate FeatureServer.
- The boundary data mixes EPA-modeled boundaries with authoritative
  state/utility-sourced boundaries. Check the `SOURCE`/`DATA_SRC` field to
  distinguish modeled estimates from verified boundaries.

# Drinking Water Violation and Compliance (SDWIS/ECHO) {#sec-sdwis}

This section mirrors the brief's Methodology subsection *Drinking Water
Violation and Compliance*. It downloads EPA's bulk Safe Drinking Water Act
(SDWA) dataset, narrows it to Cook County water systems, decodes key
fields, summarizes violations by system, and joins that summary to the
service area boundaries from @sec-boundaries.

**Sources:** EPA ECHO – SDWA Data Downloads
([summary and data dictionary](https://echo.epa.gov/tools/data-downloads/sdwa-download-summary);
[bulk download index](https://echo.epa.gov/files/echodownloads/)).

The chunk below defines the download URL and the local path for the ZIP
archive.

```{r}
#| label: sdwa-paths

zip_url  <- "https://echo.epa.gov/files/echodownloads/SDWA_latest_downloads.zip"
zip_path <- file.path(out_tabular_dir, "SDWA_latest_downloads.zip")
```

## Download the bulk SDWA dataset

The bulk dataset is a single large ZIP of CSVs (400+ MB) covering every
public water system nationally, refreshed by EPA quarterly. It is only
downloaded if a local copy is not already present; delete the ZIP to force
a refresh.

```{r}
#| label: download-sdwa

if (!file.exists(zip_path)) {
  download.file(zip_url, destfile = zip_path, mode = "wb")
}
```

## Extract required files

Only the six tables used by this pipeline are extracted. File names are
matched case-insensitively in case EPA changes casing between quarterly
releases, and any expected files that are missing are reported along with
the archive's full contents to help diagnose naming changes.

```{r}
#| label: extract-sdwa

needed_files <- c(
  "SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS.csv",
  "SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT.csv",
  "SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv",
  "SDWA_SERVICE_AREAS.csv",
  "SDWA_REF_CODE_VALUES.csv",
  "SDWA_LCR_SAMPLES.csv"          # Lead & Copper Rule sample data
)

zip_contents <- unzip(zip_path, list = TRUE)$Name

files_to_extract <- zip_contents[
  toupper(zip_contents) %in% toupper(needed_files)
]

missing <- setdiff(toupper(needed_files), toupper(files_to_extract))
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  message("Note: the following expected files were not found in this quarter's ZIP: ",
          paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
          "\nCheck zip_contents (printed below) for the current file list/naming.")
  print(zip_contents)
}

unzip(zip_path, files = files_to_extract, exdir = out_tabular_dir, overwrite = TRUE)
```

## Read and filter to Illinois

The first two characters of each `PWSID` are the state/region code (e.g.
`IL`), so every table can be filtered to Illinois systems on read, before
any joins. The helper `read_il()` does this and returns `NULL` if a file is
absent. The reference-code table is not state-specific and is small, so it
is read in full.

```{r}
#| label: read-sdwa

read_il <- function(filename) {
  path <- file.path(out_tabular_dir, filename)
  if (!file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  read_csv(path, guess_max = 100000, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
    filter(str_starts(PWSID, "IL"))
}

pws         <- read_il("SDWA_PUB_WATER_SYSTEMS.csv")
violations  <- read_il("SDWA_VIOLATIONS_ENFORCEMENT.csv")
geo_areas   <- read_il("SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv")
svc_areas   <- read_il("SDWA_SERVICE_AREAS.csv")
lcr_samples <- read_il("SDWA_LCR_SAMPLES.csv")

ref_codes <- read_csv(file.path(out_tabular_dir, "SDWA_REF_CODE_VALUES.csv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## Narrow to Cook County systems

The `COUNTY_SERVED` field in `SDWA_GEOGRAPHIC_AREAS.csv` is the most direct
way to identify Cook County systems within the Illinois subset. Because it
is self-reported by water systems and states, it may be incomplete;
discrepancies against the boundary-based approach in @sec-boundaries are
retained and reported rather than reconciled. The chunk below builds the
list of Cook County `PWSID`s and filters the system, violation, and Lead
and Copper Rule sample tables to it.

```{r}
#| label: filter-cook-county

cook_pwsids <- geo_areas %>%
  filter(str_to_upper(COUNTY_SERVED) == "COOK") %>%
  distinct(PWSID) %>%
  pull(PWSID)

message(length(cook_pwsids), " unique PWSIDs identified as serving Cook County ",
        "via the COUNTY_SERVED field.")

pws_cook        <- pws        %>% filter(PWSID %in% cook_pwsids)
violations_cook <- violations %>% filter(PWSID %in% cook_pwsids)
lcr_cook        <- lcr_samples %>% filter(PWSID %in% cook_pwsids)
```

## Decode coded fields

Violation and contaminant codes are stored as numeric/alphanumeric codes.
The helper `decode()` looks up a given `VALUE_TYPE` in the reference-code
table and joins its human-readable description onto the data as a new
column. It is applied here to add violation and contaminant descriptions.

```{r}
#| label: decode-fields

decode <- function(df, code_col, value_type, new_col) {
  lookup <- ref_codes %>%
    filter(VALUE_TYPE == value_type) %>%
    select(VALUE_CODE, VALUE_DESCRIPTION) %>%
    rename(!!new_col := VALUE_DESCRIPTION)

  df %>%
    left_join(lookup, by = setNames("VALUE_CODE", code_col))
}

violations_cook <- violations_cook %>%
  decode("VIOLATION_CODE", "VIOLATION_CODE", "violation_description") %>%
  decode("CONTAMINANT_CODE", "CONTAMINANT_CODE", "contaminant_description")
```

## Summarize violations by system

The next chunk counts, for each water system, total violations,
health-based violations, unresolved violations, and Lead and Copper Rule
violations, along with the most recent violation date. These counts are
then joined onto a subset of system attributes, with zero filled in for
systems that have no recorded violations.

Key field definitions:

- **`OWNER_TYPE_CODE`**: F = Federal, L = Local government, M =
  Public/Private, N = Native American, P = Private, S = State.
- **`RULE_CODE == "350"`** isolates Lead and Copper Rule violations.
- **`VIOLATION_STATUS`** values *Unaddressed* and *Addressed* (as opposed
  to *Resolved*/*Archived*) are treated as **unresolved**, i.e. not yet
  subject to a resolving enforcement action, per EPA's compliance status
  categories.

### Parse violation dates

`VIOL_LAST_REPORTED_DATE` is read in as a character field (EPA ECHO
exports dates as `MM/DD/YYYY`). Taking the maximum of these strings would
compare them alphabetically rather than chronologically (e.g.
`"12/01/2015"` sorts after `"01/15/2023"`), so the helper below converts
them to `Date` values *before* the most recent violation is identified.
It accepts both `MM/DD/YYYY` and ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` formats, ignores any
trailing time component, and passes through values `read_csv()` has
already parsed as dates.

```{r}
#| label: fn-parse-violation-date

parse_violation_date <- function(x) {
  if (inherits(x, "Date")) return(x)
  if (inherits(x, "POSIXt")) return(as.Date(x))
  x <- trimws(as.character(x))
  coalesce(
    as.Date(x, format = "%m/%d/%Y"),
    as.Date(x, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
  )
}
```

### Summarize by system

The chunk below computes the system-level counts and the most recent
violation date (a `Date`, or `NA` if a system has no dated violations),
then adds `most_recent_violation_year`, a numeric year derived from that
date, for filtering and mapping by year.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-violations

violation_summary <- violations_cook %>%
  mutate(viol_last_reported_date = parse_violation_date(VIOL_LAST_REPORTED_DATE)) %>%
  group_by(PWSID) %>%
  summarise(
    n_violations           = n(),
    n_health_based         = sum(IS_HEALTH_BASED_IND == "Y", na.rm = TRUE),
    n_unresolved           = sum(VIOLATION_STATUS %in% c("Unaddressed", "Addressed"), na.rm = TRUE),
    n_lead_copper_rule     = sum(RULE_CODE == "350", na.rm = TRUE),
    most_recent_violation  = if (all(is.na(viol_last_reported_date))) as.Date(NA)
                             else max(viol_last_reported_date, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(most_recent_violation_year = as.numeric(format(most_recent_violation, "%Y")))

pws_cook_summary <- pws_cook %>%
  select(PWSID, PWS_NAME, OWNER_TYPE_CODE, POPULATION_SERVED_COUNT,
         PRIMARY_SOURCE_CODE, PWS_ACTIVITY_CODE, SERVICE_CONNECTIONS_COUNT) %>%
  left_join(violation_summary, by = "PWSID") %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("n_"), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)))
```

## Save tabular outputs

The Cook County system inventory, decoded violations, Lead and Copper Rule
samples, and system-level violation summary are written to CSV.

```{r}
#| label: save-sdwa-tables

write_csv(pws_cook,         file.path(out_tabular_dir, "cook_county_pws_inventory.csv"))
write_csv(violations_cook,  file.path(out_tabular_dir, "cook_county_sdwa_violations.csv"))
write_csv(lcr_cook,         file.path(out_tabular_dir, "cook_county_lead_copper_samples.csv"))
write_csv(pws_cook_summary, file.path(out_tabular_dir, "cook_county_pws_violation_summary.csv"))
```

## Join violations to service area boundaries

This is the key spatial–tabular join. It attaches the system-level
violation summary to the service area polygons by `PWSID`, producing
`cook_cws_with_violations` — the `sf` object on which the brief's
interactive leaflet map is built. It carries `most_recent_violation` as a
`Date` and `most_recent_violation_year` as a number. The result is also
saved as a Shapefile, which shortens field names to 10 characters, so both
fields appear there under abbreviated names.

```{r}
#| label: join-violations-boundaries

cook_cws_with_violations <- cook_cws %>%
  left_join(pws_cook_summary, by = c("PWSID" = "PWSID"))

st_write(cook_cws_with_violations,
          file.path(out_spatial_dir, "cook_county_water_systems_with_violations.shp"),
          delete_dsn = TRUE)
```

## Notes

- Filtering on the `PWSID` prefix (`str_starts(PWSID, "IL")`) captures
  Illinois-primacy systems. A small number of tribal systems may be coded
  under an EPA region prefix instead; check `EPA_REGION` if tribal systems
  are in scope.
- This is quarterly-snapshot data (`SUBMISSIONYEARQUARTER` field). A
  violations *history* over time would require EPA's cumulative-year bulk
  download or the individual violations file's date fields.

# Lead Service Lines {#sec-lsl}

This section mirrors the brief's Methodology subsection *Lead Service
Lines*. It uses the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency's (IEPA)
statewide **Service Line Material Inventory Reports**, which community
water supplies submit to IEPA each year under the Lead Service Line
Replacement and Notification Act (415 ILCS 5/17.12). Each report gives a
system-level count of service lines by material (lead, galvanized, copper,
plastic, unknown, etc.), keyed to the system's `PWSID`. Because these
reports cover every community water supply in a consistent format, they
replace the earlier approach of locating and aggregating individual
municipal ArcGIS lead service line maps.

**Source:** Illinois EPA, [Lead Service Line
Information](https://epa.illinois.gov/topics/drinking-water/public-water-users/lead-service-line-information.html)
(file `ServiceLineMaterialInventoryReports.csv`).

## Locate the inventory file

The CSV is downloaded manually from the IEPA page above and saved to the
project's `data/` folder; it is not retrieved automatically. The chunk
below looks for it in `data/` relative to this document (`scripts/qmd/data/`)
and in the repository-level `data/` folder, and stops with an informative
message if it is in neither location.

```{r}
#| label: lsl-inventory-path

lsl_inventory_candidates <- c(
  file.path("data", "ServiceLineMaterialInventoryReports.csv"),
  file.path("..", "..", "data", "ServiceLineMaterialInventoryReports.csv")
)

lsl_inventory_path <- lsl_inventory_candidates[file.exists(lsl_inventory_candidates)][1]

if (is.na(lsl_inventory_path)) {
  stop("ServiceLineMaterialInventoryReports.csv was not found. Download it from ",
       "https://epa.illinois.gov/topics/drinking-water/public-water-users/lead-service-line-information.html ",
       "and save it to one of: ", paste(lsl_inventory_candidates, collapse = ", "))
}

message("Reading IEPA service line inventory from ", lsl_inventory_path)
```

## Read and filter to Cook County systems

The file contains one row per water system per reporting year
(2017–2024) for every community water supply in Illinois. It is read with
explicit column types (all count fields as integers), and the
`ReportedDate` timestamp is parsed to a date-time.

Systems are retained if IEPA lists their county as Cook **or** their
`PWSID` (`FacilityId`) appears among the Cook County systems identified
in @sec-sdwis or the service area boundaries retrieved in
@sec-boundaries. The second condition keeps systems that serve Cook
County residents but are listed under a neighboring county, so that every
mapped service area can be matched to an inventory where one exists.

```{r}
#| label: read-lsl-inventory

lsl_count_cols <- c(
  "TotalServiceConnections", "WholesaleConnections", "RetailConnections",
  "ServicesLead", "ServicesUnknownMaterial", "ServicesCopperLeadSolder",
  "ServicesGalvanized", "ServicesUnknownNotLead", "ServicesCopperNonLeadSolder",
  "ServicesCastDuctileIronTransite", "ServicesPlastic"
)

lsl_raw <- read_csv(
  lsl_inventory_path,
  col_types = cols(
    .default      = col_integer(),
    FacilityId    = col_character(),
    County        = col_character(),
    FacilityName  = col_character(),
    ReportedDate  = col_character(),
    ReportingYear = col_integer()
  )
) %>%
  mutate(ReportedDate = as.POSIXct(ReportedDate, format = "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p",
                                   tz = "America/Chicago"))

cook_lsl_pwsids <- union(cook_pwsids, cook_cws$PWSID)

lsl_cook_raw <- lsl_raw %>%
  filter(County == "Cook" | FacilityId %in% cook_lsl_pwsids) %>%
  mutate(county_listed_cook = County == "Cook")

message(n_distinct(lsl_cook_raw$FacilityId), " water systems and ",
        nrow(lsl_cook_raw), " system-year inventory reports retained for Cook County.")
```

## Standardize service line material categories

The eight material columns are collapsed into four material categories
that match the regulatory distinctions used in lead service line
replacement, plus an *unclassified* count described below:

- **Lead** (`ServicesLead`).
- **Galvanized** (`ServicesGalvanized`). Under federal and Illinois rules,
  galvanized lines that are or were downstream of lead must also be
  replaced.
- **Unknown material** (`ServicesUnknownMaterial`). These lines may be lead
  and are treated as such for replacement planning until verified.
- **Non-lead** (copper with or without lead solder, cast/ductile iron or
  transite, plastic, and "unknown but not lead").

The reporting form changed over time. Reports for 2024 include only lead
and unknown counts, with every other material column left at zero, and
some 2022 reports do not fully break down the total. Any service lines
not assigned to a material category are therefore kept in a separate
**unclassified** count (total connections minus all reported categories)
rather than assumed to be non-lead. Shares are calculated against total
service connections, and `lsl_pct_lead_or_unknown` combines lead,
galvanized, and unknown lines as the share of lines that may require
replacement.

```{r}
#| label: standardize-lsl-categories

cook_lsl_history <- lsl_cook_raw %>%
  mutate(
    lsl_total       = TotalServiceConnections,
    lsl_lead        = ServicesLead,
    lsl_galvanized  = ServicesGalvanized,
    lsl_unknown     = ServicesUnknownMaterial,
    lsl_non_lead    = ServicesCopperLeadSolder + ServicesCopperNonLeadSolder +
                      ServicesCastDuctileIronTransite + ServicesPlastic +
                      ServicesUnknownNotLead,
    lsl_unclassified = pmax(lsl_total - (lsl_lead + lsl_galvanized + lsl_unknown + lsl_non_lead), 0L),
    lsl_pct_lead            = if_else(lsl_total > 0, lsl_lead / lsl_total, NA_real_),
    lsl_pct_unknown         = if_else(lsl_total > 0, lsl_unknown / lsl_total, NA_real_),
    lsl_pct_lead_or_unknown = if_else(lsl_total > 0,
                                      (lsl_lead + lsl_galvanized + lsl_unknown) / lsl_total,
                                      NA_real_)
  ) %>%
  arrange(FacilityId, ReportingYear)
```

## Identify each system's most recent inventory

Not every system reports every year. Only about a third of Cook County
systems appear in the 2024 reports, and most systems' latest report is
from 2022. The chunk below keeps each system's most recent report
(latest `ReportingYear`, then latest `ReportedDate` if a year is
duplicated) and records which year it comes from in `lsl_reporting_year`,
so comparisons across systems can account for differences in reporting
year.

```{r}
#| label: latest-lsl-inventory

cook_lsl_latest <- cook_lsl_history %>%
  group_by(FacilityId) %>%
  arrange(desc(ReportingYear), desc(ReportedDate), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(lsl_reporting_year = ReportingYear)

print(count(cook_lsl_latest, lsl_reporting_year, name = "n_systems"))
```

## Summarize inventories by reporting year

As a quick check, the next chunk totals each material category across
Cook County systems for each reporting year. Year-to-year changes reflect
both actual replacements and reclassification of unknown lines, as well
as changes in which systems reported and in the reporting form, so these
totals are descriptive rather than a measure of replacement progress.

```{r}
#| label: lsl-summary-by-year

lsl_summary_by_year <- cook_lsl_history %>%
  group_by(ReportingYear) %>%
  summarise(
    n_systems        = n_distinct(FacilityId),
    lsl_total        = sum(lsl_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    lsl_lead         = sum(lsl_lead, na.rm = TRUE),
    lsl_galvanized   = sum(lsl_galvanized, na.rm = TRUE),
    lsl_unknown      = sum(lsl_unknown, na.rm = TRUE),
    lsl_non_lead     = sum(lsl_non_lead, na.rm = TRUE),
    lsl_unclassified = sum(lsl_unclassified, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(lsl_summary_by_year)
```

## Join inventories to service areas and save

Each system's most recent inventory is joined by `PWSID` to
`cook_cws_with_violations`, adding the `lsl_*` fields alongside the
violation summary so that lead service line prevalence can be mapped and
compared with compliance history. Service areas with no matching IEPA
report (for example, the Indiana systems) receive `NA` for these fields.
The full history, the latest-report table, and the yearly summary are
also written to CSV.

```{r}
#| label: join-save-lsl

lsl_join_fields <- cook_lsl_latest %>%
  select(PWSID = FacilityId, lsl_reporting_year, lsl_total, lsl_lead,
         lsl_galvanized, lsl_unknown, lsl_non_lead, lsl_unclassified,
         lsl_pct_lead, lsl_pct_unknown, lsl_pct_lead_or_unknown)

cook_cws_with_violations <- cook_cws_with_violations %>%
  left_join(lsl_join_fields, by = "PWSID")

message(sum(!is.na(cook_cws_with_violations$lsl_reporting_year)), " of ",
        nrow(cook_cws_with_violations), " service areas matched to an IEPA inventory report.")

write_csv(cook_lsl_history,    file.path(out_tabular_dir, "cook_county_lsl_inventory_history.csv"))
write_csv(cook_lsl_latest,     file.path(out_tabular_dir, "cook_county_lsl_inventory_latest.csv"))
write_csv(lsl_summary_by_year, file.path(out_tabular_dir, "cook_county_lsl_summary_by_year.csv"))
```

## Notes

- Inventories are system-level counts, not line-level or parcel-level
  locations, so they show how many lead lines a system has but not where
  they are within its service area.
- Counts are self-reported by water systems. Large "unknown" counts,
  especially in the 2024 reports, reflect incomplete field verification
  rather than confirmed absence or presence of lead.
- Because the reporting form changed (notably in 2024), compare material
  categories across years with caution and always note the
  `lsl_reporting_year` a figure comes from.
- Wholesale systems report wholesale connections separately
  (`WholesaleConnections`); totals here use `TotalServiceConnections` as
  reported.

# Save Essential Objects for Rendering {#sec-save}

Only the objects referenced by `drinking_water.qmd`'s evaluated
(`eval: true`) chunks are persisted, so the `.RData` file stays small and
the rendered brief depends only on what it needs:

| Object | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `cook_county` | `sf` polygon of the Cook County boundary, used as the reference outline on the brief's interactive leaflet map. |
| `cook_cws_with_violations` | `sf` polygons of community water system service areas joined to the system-level SDWA violation summary and to each system's most recent IEPA lead service line inventory (`lsl_*` fields). This is the sole data source for the interactive map (fill, hover labels, and the derived violation-density measure computed in the brief). |

All other intermediate and raw objects (`pws_cook`, `violations_cook`,
`lcr_cook`, `geo_areas`, `svc_areas`, `ref_codes`, `cook_cws`,
`cook_lsl_history`, `cook_lsl_latest`, etc.) remain available through the CSV, GeoPackage,
and Shapefile outputs written above, but are intentionally excluded from
the `.RData` file the brief loads at render time.

The final chunk saves the two essential objects with `xz` compression.

```{r}
#| label: save-rdata

save(cook_county, cook_cws_with_violations, file = out_rdata_path, compress = "xz")

message("Saved essential rendering data (cook_county, cook_cws_with_violations) to ",
        out_rdata_path)
```
